Vocabulary · Lesson 16

Feelings & personality

Say how you feel and describe what people are like. Learn feeling adjectives with be and feel, escape the classic bored / boring trap, and build a set of personality words for real people in your life: I feel nervous, The meeting was boring, She’s friendly and hard-working.

≈ 50–60 min -ed vs -ing feeling vs personality 11 interactive tasks
NoticeRead a short message about a new job.
DiscoverFeelings now vs. what a person is like.
BuildChoose, type, build, and repair.
UseDescribe yourself and people you know.

Two key questions: How do you feel? asks about your feeling right now. What’s she like? asks about her personality. Careful: What does she like? is a different question. It asks about things she enjoys.

Notice before the rule

Read Dana’s message about her new job

“How do you feel about the new job? · Honestly, I’m excited, but a little nervous too. The training was long and tiring, and by the end I felt bored. But my manager is friendly and patient, so I think it will be fine.”

  • Look at I felt bored and the training was tiring. One word describes a person’s feeling, the other describes the thing that causes it. Which ending goes with which?
  • Dana says I’m excited and I felt bored. So which verbs can go before a feeling adjective?
  • Her manager is friendly and patient. Is that how the manager feels today, or what the manager is usually like?

Discovery check: read the cue, then choose

Use -ed for how a person feels and -ing for the thing that causes the feeling. For feelings, be and feel both work.

1I nervous before interviews.  (after I · verb + feeling adjective)
2The movie was slow and , so we left early.  (bored / boring · the movie causes it)
3We were after ten minutes.  (bored / boring · how the people felt)
4My commute is long and .  (tired / tiring · the commute causes it)
5I’m always after that commute.  (tired / tiring · how I feel)
6Marta friendly and patient.  (be + adjective · her usual personality)

The system: -ed for the person, -ing for the cause

Feeling adjectives go after be or feel: I’m nervous. = I feel nervous. Both are correct and natural.

Some feeling adjectives come in pairs. The -ed form describes how a person feels. The -ing form describes the thing that causes the feeling. This is the classic trap at this level, so learn the pairs as chunks:

-ed · how a person feels-ing · the thing that causes it
I’m bored.  the personThe meeting is boring.  the meeting
She’s interested in the project.The project is interesting.
We were tired after the trip.The trip was tiring.
He was surprised by the news.The news was surprising.

Meaning check

  • Say I’m boring and you are describing your personality as dull. Say I’m bored and you are describing your feeling right now. Big difference!
  • Feelings change: today, right now, this week. Use be or feel: I’m worried about the deadline. I feel calm now.
  • For past feelings, use past forms: I was embarrassed. I felt nervous before the interview.

Personality: usually true, not just today

Personality adjectives describe what a person is usually like, not how they feel at one moment. Ten useful ones:

wordmeaningwordmeaning
friendlywarm and open with peoplehonesttells the truth
funnymakes people laughhard-workingputs real effort into work
quietdoesn’t talk muchlazyavoids work or effort
kindcares about other peopleshynervous with new people
patientcan wait and repeat calmlytalkativetalks a lot

Keep the two ideas apart. Personality is usually true; a feeling is right now:

personality · usually truefeeling · right now
She’s friendly.  with everyone, alwaysShe’s nervous.  today, before the interview
He’s quiet.  his characterHe’s tired.  after a long shift
They’re hard-working.  in generalThey’re excited.  about the trip next week

Two questions that look alike

  • What’s she like? asks about personality: She’s kind and a little shy. The like here is not the verb for enjoying things.
  • What does she like? asks about things she enjoys: She likes coffee and hiking.
  • For feelings, ask How do you feel? or How are you feeling?: I feel a little worried, honestly.

Choose the word that fits the person

Drill 1: feeling or personality?

Read the whole sentence first. Is it about a feeling right now, a thing that causes a feeling, or what someone is usually like?

1The training video was three hours long. Everyone was by the end.  (bored / boring · how the people felt)
2The new project is really . I want to learn more about it.  (interested / interesting · the project causes it)
3I felt before my presentation, so I took a deep breath.  (feeling · worried before something important)
4Our manager never shouts. She stays under pressure.  (= relaxed, not stressed)
5My colleague explains things twice without a problem. He’s very .  (= can wait and repeat calmly)
6Elena chats with everyone at lunch. She’s the most person on the team.  (= talks a lot)
7Sami doesn’t say much in big meetings. He’s a little with new people.  (= nervous with new people)
8It was very of you to help me move on Saturday. Thank you!  (= caring about others)

Drill 2: type the missing word

Type one word. Use -ed for the person’s feeling and -ing for the thing that causes it. The cue in parentheses helps you choose.

1The conference was tiring, and now I feel really .  (tired / tiring)
2My new job isn’t boring at all. It’s really .  (interested / interesting)
3Two hours of delays at the airport! We were so .  (bored / boring)
4He always tells the truth, even when it’s hard. He’s very .  (personality · tells the truth)
5My brother never does his dishes. He’s so .  (personality · avoids work)
6A: How do you today?  B: I feel much better, thanks.  (the question for feelings)

Build the meaning, then the sentence

Drill 3: describe a coworker’s personality

Your coworker Marta helps everyone and always finishes her projects. Build the sentence, then say it.

Drill 4: build the past feeling

Talk about a feeling in the past with felt. Build the sentence, then say it.

Notice and repair errors

Drill 5: who feels it, what causes it?

Tap the word that is wrong. Think: is the meeting a person with feelings?

Drill 6: adjective before the noun

Tap the word that is wrong. Which word describes person?

Drill 7: transform it aloud, then reveal

Say the new sentence aloud first. Reveal only after you answer.

1 I’m bored.  →  now describe the movie instead

The movie is boring.

2 She is nervous today.  →  move it to yesterday

She was nervous yesterday.

3 He talks a lot.  →  say it with one personality word

He’s talkative.

4 What does she like?  →  ask about her personality instead

What’s she like?

5 The trip was tiring.  →  say how you felt after it, with feel in the past

I felt tired.

6 How do you feel?  →  ask me about my usual personality instead

What are you like?

Read and choose

Dana’s message after week one

“First week at the new office! My manager, Priya, is kind and really patient. She explained the systems twice and never got annoyed. The guy next to me, Tom, is quiet at first, but he’s actually very funny. Today was stressful, though: the printer broke before a big meeting, and my laptop started playing music in front of everyone. I felt so embarrassed! By six I was completely tired, but honestly? I’m excited about this job.”

Read, then choose

1. What’s Priya like?

2. How did Dana feel when her laptop played music?

3. Which sentence is true?

Use it in real life

Right now: Say how you feel today and why, in two sentences. I feel a little tired because I worked late. But I’m excited about the weekend.
Your best friend: Describe your best friend’s personality with three adjectives, then give one example. She’s funny, honest, and a little talkative. Last week she made the whole table laugh.
A nervous moment: Tell a short story about a time you felt nervous. Use the past simple. I felt nervous before my first job interview. My hands were cold, but the manager was friendly, and I got the job.
Interview the teacher: Ask the teacher What are you like? and one follow-up question. Then answer the same questions yourself. What are you like? Are you patient with slow learners?
Two people you know: Compare the personalities of two people in your life. My father is quiet and calm, but my uncle is talkative and funny. They’re both kind.

Reflect

Explain the system

Complete this aloud: “The -ed form describes how a ______ feels. The -ing form describes the ______ that causes the feeling. What’s she like? asks about her ______, but What does she like? asks about things she ______.”

Then say one true sentence about how you feel right now and one true sentence about what you are usually like.

1. The lecture was really ___, so half the class fell asleep.

2. You want to know about your new manager’s personality. What do you ask?

3. He never lies, even when the truth is difficult. He’s very ___.

4. I ___ nervous before the test last month, but I passed.

5. Sofia chats with everyone at every party. She’s really ___.

6. My coworker can explain the same thing five times without getting angry. He’s so ___.

7. A: How do you feel?  B: ___
